Programming the IoT: MicroPython & Arduino

Every chapter so far has described the sense → process → act loop in the abstract. This chapter is where you actually write it: first in MicroPython, running Python directly on a microcontroller, then in Arduino's C-based sketch format. Same loop, two languages, two very different sets of trade-offs.

Title slide (blank capture)
Instructor title slide
Slide number only
Security-use notice, repeat

What is MicroPython, and why use it here?

MicroPython is a lean implementation of Python 3, carrying a small subset of the standard library, optimized to run directly on microcontrollers and other constrained environments. It was created by Damien George and first released in 2014. The line worth sitting with: the same language you use on a desktop can now run directly on a microcontroller with kilobytes of RAM — the ESP32 from Chapter 4, with its 520 KB of SRAM, runs an actual Python interpreter, not a simulation of one.

Embedded development has traditionally meant C or assembly — manual memory management, a steep learning curve. MicroPython lets you focus on the IoT logic itself (reading sensors, making decisions, sending data) before confronting those low-level details. Its interactive REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) means you can read a sensor value and print it with a single typed line — no compile-and-flash cycle standing between you and seeing a result.

AspectCPythonMicroPython
Runs onDesktop / laptop / serverMicrocontrollers (ESP32, RP2040, …)
Memory footprintTens of MBTens of KB
Standard libraryFullA subset (micropython-lib adds more)
REPLYesYes (over USB serial)
File I/ODisk filesOn-board flash filesystem
Why this matters given Chapter 4 MicroPython's "tens of KB" footprint is only possible because of the trade-offs Chapter 4 described for Cortex-M-class chips: no MMU, no full OS, a single program running directly on the hardware. MicroPython isn't Python plus an operating system underneath — the interpreter itself effectively is the operating system for that chip while it runs. That's also why the standard library is trimmed to a subset: there's no disk, no multiprocessing, no other programs to coordinate with, so entire chunks of CPython's library have nothing to do on a microcontroller.

Setting up Thonny

Thonny is the IDE used to write and run MicroPython in this course. On Windows: download the installer from thonny.org, accept the defaults (it bundles its own Python, so nothing separate needs installing), then launch it from the Start menu. macOS follows the same shape with a .pkg installer.

1Open Thonny — you'll see an editor pane on top and a Shell pane below.
2Run → Select interpreter…
3Choose "The same interpreter which runs Thonny (default)."
4Click OK — the Shell should now show a Python version line beginning with >>>.

The setup check has two parts. First, type directly into the Shell at the >>> prompt — this is the REPL in action:

>>> 2 + 3
>>> print("MicroPython is ready")

Then, in the editor pane, write a short script and save it as setup_check.py before running it with F5 (this is the compile-and-flash-free workflow the REPL made possible, now used for a slightly longer program than a single line):

student_name = "Your Name Here"
print("Setup check passed for", student_name)

total = 0
for i in range(1, 6):
    total += i
print("Sum of 1..5 is", total)

Your first MicroPython program

# first_program.py
# Announce the device and report the current time.
import time

DEVICE_ID = "IoT-Station-01"

def boot_message(device):
    print("=" * 30)
    print(device, "booting...")
    print("Time now:", time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S'))
    print("=" * 30)

boot_message(DEVICE_ID)

Small as it is, this program already demonstrates the shape every later sketch follows: a named constant identifying the device (DEVICE_ID — this is the "unique identity" requirement from Chapter 3's smart-object definition, now literally a line of code), a function that does the actual work, and a single call that runs it. Every guided task below adds one more piece on top of this same skeleton.

Guided tasks

Task 1 — Variables, input, and output

The task statement makes an important point explicit: a sensor reading is just a number stored in a variable. Whether that number comes from a keyboard or a DHT22 temperature sensor, the code that stores and prints it is identical. This is worth internalizing before writing any sensor code at all — you're never really writing "sensor code," you're writing ordinary variable-and-print code that happens to receive its input from a physical sensor instead of a keyboard.

Task 2 — Control flow and functions

# task2_control_flow.py
# Classify simulated sensor readings against a threshold.
def classify(reading, threshold, band=2.0):
    """Return 'LOW', 'OK', or 'HIGH' for a reading vs threshold."""
    if reading < threshold - band:
        return "LOW"
    elif reading > threshold + band:
        return "HIGH"
    else:
        return "OK"

THRESHOLD = 28.0
readings = [24.0, 26.1, 29.8, 30.5, 22.7]

high_count = 0
for i, r in enumerate(readings):
    status = classify(r, THRESHOLD)
    print("Reading", i, "=", r, "->", status)
    if status == "HIGH":
        high_count += 1

print("Total HIGH readings:", high_count)

The band parameter is doing real engineering work, not just tidiness: without it, a reading sitting exactly at the threshold would flip between LOW/OK/HIGH on the tiniest noise. Building a tolerance band around the threshold is a small-scale preview of the hysteresis concept the additional tasks introduce properly below.

Task 3 — Simulating and processing sensor data

# task3_sensor_data.py
# Simulate readings, summarise, and export as JSON.
import random
import json

def simulate_reading(base, jitter):
    """Return a simulated reading around base +/- jitter."""
    return round(base + random.uniform(-jitter, jitter), 2)

BASE_TEMP = 27.0
JITTER = 1.5
SAMPLES = 10

readings = [simulate_reading(BASE_TEMP, JITTER) for _ in range(SAMPLES)]

avg = round(sum(readings) / len(readings), 2)
mn = min(readings)
mx = max(readings)

print("Readings:", readings)
print("Average:", avg, "| Min:", mn, "| Max:", mx)

payload = {
    "sensor": "temperature",
    "count": len(readings),
    # ... avg/min/max keys continue below the slide's crop
}

This task is the whole point of Chapter 1's "IoT and the rise of time-series data" argument, written as eleven lines of code: readings is a time series, avg/min/max are the simplest possible analytics on it, and packaging the summary as a payload dictionary bound for json.dumps() is precisely how a real device would format data before sending it over MQTT or HTTP to the cloud layer from Chapter 2's architecture.

Additional tasks

Three extensions build directly on Task 3:

ExtensionWhat's new
Two sensors at onceSimulate temperature and humidity separately, then combine both summaries into one JSON object: {"temperature": {...}, "humidity": {...}}
Hysteresis over a streamLoop over 20 simulated readings; raise an alarm only when a reading goes HIGH, and don't raise it again until a reading returns to OK first
CSV loggingWrite 15 readings to log.csv as timestamp,reading lines, then read the file back to confirm it was written correctly
Hysteresis: the counterintuitive-sounding fix for a very real bug Imagine a temperature alarm that fires the instant a reading exceeds 30°C and clears the instant it drops back below 30°C. If the true temperature is hovering at exactly 30.0°C with normal sensor noise, the alarm will flicker on and off dozens of times per second — a phenomenon called flapping. Hysteresis fixes this by requiring the reading to cross back to OK before the alarm can fire again — the alarm "remembers" it already fired and won't re-fire on noise alone. This is exactly the same band-around-a-threshold idea from Task 2's classify() function, just applied across time instead of across a single reading.

Build it together: the "Heartbeat" — onboard LED control

The first hands-on-hardware task: create a project folder, add the machine.py module your instructor provides, then write:

from machine import Pin

led = Pin("LED", Pin.OUT)  # onboard LED
led.value(1)

This is the first line of code in the whole chapter that touches physical hardware, and it's worth noticing what changed: machine.Pin is MicroPython's interface to a literal GPIO pin — the same GPIO concept from Chapter 4's ESP32 pinout diagram, now addressed by name from Python rather than by a datasheet pin number.

Make it blink

from machine import Pin
from time import sleep

led = Pin("LED", Pin.OUT)
while True:
    led.toggle()  # flip it
    sleep(0.5)    # wait half a second

while True is the MicroPython equivalent of Chapter 4's "the loop runs forever" idea — an embedded program has no natural endpoint, because the physical system it's controlling doesn't stop existing when the code would otherwise finish.

Say what's happening

from machine import Pin
from time import sleep

led = Pin("LED", Pin.OUT)
while True:
    led.toggle()
    print("LED state:", led.value())  # 1 or 0
    sleep(0)

Count the beats

from machine import Pin
from time import sleep

led = Pin("LED", Pin.OUT)
count = 0                          # remembers the beat number

def heartbeat(n):                  # a reusable block; n = the beat number
    led.toggle()
    print("Beat", n, "- LED:", led.value())

while True:
    count = count + 1              # add 1 each time round
    heartbeat(count)
    sleep(0.5)

This is the exact same blink-and-print behavior as the previous two slides, refactored into a function with a persistent count variable — the natural next step once a piece of logic (announcing a beat) is going to be reused, exactly the same instinct that produced classify() and simulate_reading() as functions earlier in this chapter.

Task 1 — SOS blinker

Goal: blink Morse code for SOS — three short blinks (0.2s on), three long blinks (0.6s on), three short, then a 2s pause before repeating. The suggested approach is a small helper blink(on_time) that turns the LED on for on_time then off for a short gap, called inside three separate for _ in range(3): loops (one per letter). A working version should print 9 on/off pairs (short, long, short) before each pause.

Embedded C & Arduino

Embedded C is a variant of C used to program microcontrollers directly. Unlike desktop C, embedded C programs run on bare metal with severely limited RAM (the Arduino Uno from Chapter 3 has just 2 KB), no operating system underneath, and direct access to hardware pins — there's no filesystem, no process scheduler, nothing standing between your code and the chip.

The Arduino platform — board, language, and IDE together — was designed in 2005 at the Ivrea Interaction Design Institute specifically so artists and students could build interactive projects without an electronics background. It hides bare-metal AVR register programming behind simple functions like digitalWrite() and analogRead(), letting you focus on IoT logic first — the exact same motivation MicroPython gave for using Python on a microcontroller, just solved with a simplified C API instead of a whole different language. And critically: the same code compiles and runs unchanged on the real physical board.

Every Arduino program ("sketch") requires exactly two functions: setup(), which runs once at power-on, and loop(), which repeats forever. This mirrors the real-time nature of embedded systems from Chapter 4: initialize once, then respond continuously — the C equivalent of MicroPython's "define your pins, then while True."

Setting up Tinkercad Circuits

Tinkercad Circuits is a free, browser-based simulator from Autodesk. You drag a virtual Arduino Uno and components onto a breadboard, write code in the built-in editor, and click Start Simulation — the Serial Monitor and component animations behave like the real hardware, with no software install required.

1Go to tinkercad.com and sign up (personal or institutional email).
2Verify your email, then log in.
3Click "Circuits" in the sidebar (under "Show all" if needed).
4Click "Create new Circuit" for a blank breadboard workspace.

Drag an "Arduino Uno R3" onto the workspace, click it to reveal the code panel, and switch the language selector from "Blocks" to "Text" to write real Arduino C — the block-based mode exists but this course works directly in text/C.

ComponentSearch termUsed in
LEDLEDTask 1 — digital output
Resistor (220Ω)ResistorTask 1 — current limiting for the LED
Breadboard SmallBreadboardAll tasks — wiring surface
PotentiometerPotentiometerTask 2 — analog input
PushbuttonPushbuttonAdditional task — digital input
Piezo (buzzer)PiezoAdditional task — PWM/tone output

Anatomy of an Arduino sketch

// --- 1. Global declarations (variables, pin numbers, constants) ---
const int LED_PIN = 13;        // pin number as a named constant

// --- 2. setup() — runs once at power-on ---
void setup() {
  pinMode(LED_PIN, OUTPUT);    // configure the pin as an output
  Serial.begin(9600);          // start serial communication at 9600 baud
}

// --- 3. loop() — runs forever ---
void loop() {
  digitalWrite(LED_PIN, HIGH); // turn the LED on
  delay(500);                  // wait 500 milliseconds
  digitalWrite(LED_PIN, LOW);  // turn the LED off
  delay(500);                  // wait 500 milliseconds
}
PartWhen it runsWhat goes here
Global declarationsCompiled before anything runsPin constants, global variables, #includes, function prototypes
setup()Once, at power-on or resetPin mode configuration, Serial.begin, sensor initialization
loop()Repeatedly, foreverThe main program logic — read sensors, decide, actuate, send data

Notice this is exactly the sensor → controller → actuator loop from Chapter 3, mapped directly onto loop()'s job description: read sensors (sense), make decisions (the controller step), actuate outputs (the actuator step), all repeating forever.

Key Arduino functions

FunctionWhat it does
pinMode(pin, mode)Configures a pin as INPUT, OUTPUT, or INPUT_PULLUP. Called in setup().
digitalWrite(pin, value)Sets a digital pin HIGH (5V) or LOW (0V). Only works on OUTPUT pins.
digitalRead(pin)Reads a digital pin: returns HIGH or LOW.
analogRead(pin)Reads an analog pin (A0–A5): returns 0–1023 for 0–5V (10-bit resolution — the same "resolution" metric defined in Chapter 3).
analogWrite(pin, value)Outputs a PWM signal (0–255) on ~-marked pins — dimming LEDs or setting motor speed.
delay(ms)Pauses for ms milliseconds — blocking; nothing else runs meanwhile.
Serial.begin(baud)Starts serial communication; 9600 is the standard rate used throughout.
Serial.print / println(data)Prints to the Serial Monitor, with or without a trailing newline.
map(val, fromLow, fromHigh, toLow, toHigh)Re-maps a number from one range to another, e.g. 0–1023 to 0–100.
analogRead's 1024 possible values is Chapter 3's resolution metric, not a coincidence The Arduino Uno's ADC is 10-bit, meaning it can represent 2¹⁰ = 1024 distinct values (0–1023) across whatever voltage range it's reading. That number is the sensor chain's resolution, in the exact sense Chapter 3 defined it: the smallest distinguishable step in the measured quantity. A 5V range split across 1024 steps means each step represents about 4.9 mV — any real-world voltage change smaller than that is invisible to analogRead(), no matter how good the sensor attached to the pin is.

Arduino: first programs & tasks

Click "Start Simulation" in Tinkercad — if a default blinking-LED sketch is loaded, pin 13's LED should flash. Click "Stop Simulation" to halt it.

// setup_check.ino
// Confirm Tinkercad simulation and Serial Monitor are working.

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  Serial.println("Embedded C is ready");
}

void loop() {
  // nothing here yet
}
// loop_check.ino
// Confirm loop() runs continuously.

int counter = 0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  Serial.print("Loop iteration: ");
  Serial.println(counter);
  counter = counter + 1;
  delay(1000);
}

This is the same "count the beats" idea from the MicroPython Heartbeat section, in Arduino C: a persistent variable, incremented once per pass through the infinite loop, with a delay controlling the pace.

// first_program.ino
// Announce the device and blink the on-board LED.

const int LED_PIN = 13;
const char DEVICE_ID[] = "IoT-Station-01";

void setup() {
  pinMode(LED_PIN, OUTPUT);
  Serial.begin(9600);
  Serial.println("========================================");
  Serial.print(DEVICE_ID);
  Serial.println(" booting...");
  Serial.println("========================================");
}

void loop() {
  digitalWrite(LED_PIN, HIGH);
  delay(500);
  digitalWrite(LED_PIN, LOW);
  delay(500);
}

Compare this directly against the MicroPython first_program.py from earlier in this chapter — same DEVICE_ID constant, same boot-announcement banner, same blink behavior. This side-by-side is the whole chapter's thesis made visible: the underlying IoT logic (announce yourself, then loop forever reacting to the world) doesn't change between languages — only the syntax carrying it does.

Additional Task — Button-controlled LED

Wire a pushbutton to digital pin 2 (with a 10KΩ pull-down resistor to GND, and the other side to 5V) and an LED to pin 8. Write a program that turns the LED on while the button is held and off when released, printing "Button: PRESSED" or "Button: RELEASED" only on each change of state — not continuously on every loop pass. That last requirement forces you to track the previous state in a variable and compare it against the current reading each time through loop(), the same "detect a change, not just a level" logic behind the hysteresis task earlier in this chapter.

Additional Task B — Threshold alarm

Using the potentiometer on A0 from Task 2, set a threshold of 512 (roughly the midpoint of the 0–1023 ADC range, i.e. about 2.5V). When the reading exceeds 512: blink the onboard LED rapidly (100ms on/off) and print "ALARM: threshold exceeded". When below 512: keep the LED off and print "OK" once every 2 seconds. This is Task 2's MicroPython classify() function again — a threshold comparison driving a visible actuator response — now wired to an actual analog sensor and a real LED instead of a simulated list of numbers.

The thread connecting this entire unit, end to end: Chapter 1 defined the sense/connect/process/act pipeline. Chapter 2 gave it a formal, layered architecture. Chapter 3 opened up the sensors and actuators sitting at that architecture's bottom layer. Chapter 4 opened up the chip that reads those sensors and drives those actuators. This chapter closes the loop by putting real code — in two different languages — on that exact chip, doing exactly that job. Everything you've built here, from a temperature threshold alarm to a button-controlled LED, is a complete, working, miniature instance of the same "smart object" this whole unit has been describing from six different angles.
